t: Everything alive is written with four letters. An oak tree, a shark, you. The same four.
One alphabet, four letters, and every living thing that has ever existed is written in it — including the ones nobody has found yet.
Four bases, universal across every domain of life. The alphabet is not merely similar between organisms; it is identical.

Four nucleotides, and a coding convention shared by essentially every organism on earth. Universality of that kind is a fact that demands an explanation, and it is one of the few facts every account of life's history has to accommodate.
sub: Twenty-six letters seem barely enough for English. Four run everything.
The question worth holding: is four a lot or hardly any?
Information capacity is set by alphabet size and string length together, and the second term is doing nearly all the work.

question: Can you write much with only four letters?
Is a four-letter alphabet enough to specify an organism?
options: Yes, if the message is long enough
No, four is far too few
stages.outcome: Yes, if the message is long enough
note: Commit. A computer manages with two, which is a hint about which term matters.

stages.label: How long is the message?
captions: 30 letters: more than a billion billion.
t: Four letters is not many. But watch what happens when the message gets longer.
Alphabet size adds; message length multiplies. Watch which one wins.
after: Every letter you add multiplies the possibilities by four. Your genome is three billion letters long — the number of possible sequences that length is beyond any use for a number.

t: The four letters are A, T, C and G. They are called bases.
The four letters are A, T, C and G — adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. Each is a base.
Adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine: two purines and two pyrimidines, strung along a sugar-phosphate backbone.
The backbone is chemically uniform, which matters: the sequence carries the information precisely because the chemistry does not constrain the order. Any base can follow any base.
sub: And they always hold hands the same way: A with T, C with G.
They pair in a fixed way — A always with T, C always with G. That is the next lesson, and it is the important one.
Pairing is A–T and C–G, enforced by geometry: a purine always faces a pyrimidine, so every rung spans the same distance.
Chargaff noticed the ratios A=T and C=G years before anyone knew why. The explanation, when it arrived, was the structure — and it carried the copying mechanism with it.

t: Put each letter next to the one it holds hands with.
Match each base with its partner.
Any base will go in any slot here, so getting it right is up to you.
Placement is unconstrained — any base fits any position, and only the assignment is graded. Pair them correctly.

q: Why is a four-base alphabet sufficient?
Why is alphabet size the wrong thing to worry about?
options: Because the message is billions of letters long
Because each letter means a lot on its own
why: Each extra letter multiplies what you can say by four. Make the message long enough and four letters can say anything.
Capacity grows exponentially with length and only linearly with alphabet size. Three billion positions at four options each is capacity nobody has found a use for all of.

This is why binary is not a limitation for computers either. The alphabet sets bits per symbol — two for DNA — and the length does the rest. The interesting constraints on genomes are error rate and replication cost, not vocabulary.

t: Because it is the same four letters in everything, you can put a human instruction into a bacterium and it works.

Universality is what makes biotechnology possible at all: a human insulin gene placed in E. coli is read correctly, because the alphabet and very nearly the whole coding convention are shared. Nothing has to be translated.

q: Which letter does C hold hands with?
What is the complement of cytosine?
why: C always goes with G, and A always goes with T. Never any other way round.
C pairs with G, A with T. The rule has no exceptions, and the next lesson is about what that rule makes possible.

C–G, joined by three hydrogen bonds against A–T's two, which is why GC-rich sequence has a higher melting temperature. The pairing is geometric as well as chemical: purine to pyrimidine keeps every rung the same width.
